about: The hand-written parts of models/: what each task takes and is scored against, and this agent's reading. The reading is a hypothesis from small samples; tools/models-report.mjs puts it on the pages beside the figures.
label: hypothesis
how_to_read: With 10 to 20 items a task, one item is 5 to 10 points: a model at 17 of 20 and one at 16 of 20 are not told apart by this. What round 1 does show: the copy-a-field task is too easy to separate anything (every model, every item); the smallest models fall away as soon as a rule has to be applied; and the price for the same answers differs by a factor of about a hundred, mostly because some models reason at length by default. **Round 2 is partial.** Round 2 (from 02:53 UTC: a harder warnings task, all 46 timeline rows, three whole paragraphs to translate, each item three times, reasoning on and off as separate rows) stopped part-way: from 02:55 UTC OpenRouter refused every call with 'Insufficient credits' (the account's balance, not this team's cap: the team had spent about a dollar). Refused calls are not answers and are not in the results. What completed is shown and marked partial; the rest runs when the account has credits. The one new task that ran far enough to read, warnings in force at an hour, does separate the models: see its page.

extract-warning.input: An IPMA CAP message (event, onset, expires, area and description in Portuguese), as kept in `weather/cap.json`
extract-warning.gold: The same record's type, level, area, start and end, normalised (`weather/cap.json`)
extract-warning.reading: Every model got every item. As built, the task is a copy with a small translation (Vermelho to red, +00:00 to Z) and it separates nothing. It does say the cheapest open-weight model here can turn a CAP message into our fields for about 0.00002 US dollars an item. A harder second version is the next step: the warning as a sentence in IPMA's communiqué, several warnings in one text, and local time in summer.

extract-decision.input: A short official passage (the government's declaration, IPMA's CAP message or communiqué, one quoted line of an organiser's or operator's own page), with where it was published
extract-decision.gold: The decision graph's edge: its decider and effect window, null where the source states no clock hour (`decisions/graph.json`); for two CAP messages with no edge, the message's own onset and expires
extract-decision.reading: The errors are of two kinds, and both are the ones a curator must not make. Inventing hours: asked for the window of IPMA's communiqué sentence, which gives none, three small models filled in the communiqué's issue time, and one gave the metro's 'nights of 10 to 11 and 11 to 12' clock hours it does not state. Naming the wrong decider: two models gave the Government for Web Summit's own sentence 'will respect the Government's direction, and accordingly, Day 2 will not take place' (the organisers decided; the government advised), and the smallest gave Madeira's civil protection for IPMA's warnings in Madeira. Ten items: enough to see the kinds of error, not to rank the models that made none.

label.input: A row of our timeline (its text without the leading 'signal:' or 'analysis' marker) and its source labels (`signals.json`)
label.gold: The row's label in `signals.json`: fact, evidence or hypothesis
label.reading: No model passed 17 of 20, and the misses are mostly the same rows for every model, which points at our labels as much as at the models. Two rows the lead marks 'analysis' (so: hypothesis) are counts made by incident.media@ from its own dataset (who published when; that no title had reported a change by a given time): 13 of 13 and 11 of 13 models call them fact or evidence. One team row ('No further statement from Web Summit', from a watcher's sweep) split the models three ways. The clear rows (IPMA's own data; a forecast-like reading by the meteorologist; a press report relayed by a watcher) were labelled right by nearly every model above the smallest. The smallest model (4 billion parameters) got 8 of 20: not usable for this.

translate.input: IPMA's Portuguese warning text, or one sentence of its communiqué no. 2 (`weather/cap.json`, `warnings.json`, `communiques.json`)
translate.gold: The figures and units of the Portuguese text itself; there is no reference translation
translate.reading: Nine of thirteen models kept every figure and unit in all 20 texts, the 4-billion-parameter one among them. The failures were not mistranslations: one small model answered with nested JSON instead of a sentence (0 of 20 by our format rule, though the figures were in it), and the models that reason by default ran out of 4,000 tokens before answering on some of the longer sentences. What this check cannot see: whether the English is right. A wrong word with the right numbers passes. That needs a second check (a back-translation compared by a person, or IPMA's own English pages where they exist).

warnings-in-force.input: All seventeen CAP messages held for the Lisbon district, oldest first, and one hour of 11 or 12 November (`weather/cap.json`)
warnings-in-force.gold: The warnings in force at that hour by IPMA's own warnings API as read (`weather/warnings.json`): type, level, end
warnings-in-force.reading: Partial: the account ran out of credits while this task was running, so only three rows have all 13 items three times, and several have a handful. What there is: this task separates models that the copy-a-field task could not. `google/gemma-4-31b-it` got the same 11 of 13 in each of three runs; `meta-llama/llama-4-maverick`, its equal on every round-1 task, got 1 or 2 of 13; the small models got none. Where a row was asked with reasoning on, it did better than the same model with it off (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 11 of 11 on, 5 of the 8 items it reached off; Gemma 4 10 of 10 on) at three to four times the price per item and 7 to 23 seconds instead of 1 to 2. These are counts from an unfinished run: enough to say the task is worth finishing, not to rank.

use.job: Turning a structured official message (CAP, IPMA's JSON) into our fields
use.pick: a small open-weight model (`google/gemma-3-4b-it`, or `google/gemma-4-31b-it` for a margin), or no model at all:
use.why: the cheapest got 17 of 17, and a parser does this for nothing and cannot be wrong in new ways. A model earns its place only when the text is prose.

use.job: Extracting who decided and for which hours from official prose
use.pick: a large open-weight model (`google/gemma-4-31b-it`, `meta-llama/llama-4-maverick`, `deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash`) or a cheap commercial one (`google/gemini-3.5-flash-lite`, `anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5`):
use.why: each got 10 of 10 at 0.0001 to 0.0005 US dollars an item. Not the models under about 10 billion parameters: they invent hours. Whatever the model, a null window stays null until a person or the source fills it.

use.job: A first translation of IPMA's warning text for the English gloss the Weather face asks for
use.why: with the figures check run on every output and the Portuguese always shown beside it. IPMA's text is the warning; the English is a reading aid and says so.

the best agree with our labels on 17 of 20 and the disagreements are informative. Useful now as a second reader that flags rows where several models disagree with the lead's label, for the lead to look at; never as the labeller.

use.job: Anything in a loop, every few minutes
use.pick: not the models that reason by default (`qwen/qwen3.5-397b-a17b`, `mistralai/mistral-large-4-0`, `qwen/qwen3.5-9b`) at their default settings:
use.why: for the same answers they took 10 to 30 seconds an item and the two large ones cost more than the other eleven models together. Asked not to reason (the rows marked `#reasoning-off`), the two Qwen models cost a fifteenth to a seventieth as much. The small one did as well on translation (20 of 20, having stopped running out of tokens) and worse where a rule is weighed (labels 12 to 10 of 20, decisions 9 to 6 of 10). The large one did as well everywhere it answered: decisions 10 of 10, translation 17 of 17, labels 12 of 15 against 16 of 20 with reasoning. **A correction:** at 02:39 UTC this page said the large one fell from 16 to 12 of 20 on labels; five of those 20 calls had been refused by the provider for lack of credits and were counted as wrong answers. They are now left out. Mistral Large 4, GPT-OSS 20B and Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite reason whatever they are told (the provider refuses the setting).

use.job: What other sources and answer engines say (the shadow report)
use.pick: an answer engine with search (`perplexity/sonar`, about half a cent a question in one test call),
use.why: through the same wrapper, its answer kept as evidence about the engine, with the pages it cites. Measured by incident.shadow@, not here: its first round is at shadow/.

own_data: The label task doubles as a check of the timeline, and it found a gap in our labels rather than a wrong label: on three rows most models disagree with the lead's label, and all three are things we counted or observed ourselves (s-1110T2358, s-1111T0015, s-1110T2153). The lead keeps the labels; the question it raises for Dinis, with each row and each model's answer, is on the label page.
more_would_buy: **The budget.** The team's cap is 20 US dollars a day from 02:50 UTC on 11 November (5 before); this desk's share is 6 and it has spent about 0.87. Round 2 in full (109 items, 20 rows, three runs of the cheap rows) is about 2 to 3 dollars. It needs credits on the OpenRouter account first: the account's balance, which is not ours to top up, ran out at 02:55 UTC.
which_about: For the other agents: which model to call for which job on this site, from round 1. Our choice, a hypothesis from small samples; the figures beside each are that model's on the task named. Every call through tools/models-ask.mjs or tools/llm.mjs; reasoning off unless the row says otherwise; a model's output never reaches a page without the check in the last column.

which.job: A CAP message or IPMA's JSON into our fields
which.check: the parser's own tests; a model only when the text is prose

which.job: A warning or decision in official prose into fields (who, hours)
which.check: a second model (`google/gemini-3.5-flash-lite`) on the same text; where the two differ, a person reads the source. A null hour stays null

which.job: English gloss of IPMA's Portuguese warning text
which.check: the figures check (every number and unit of the Portuguese in the English); the Portuguese always shown beside it

which.job: The same gloss, at volume (thousands of texts)
which.check: the figures check; not for anything but translation (8 of 20 on labels, 3 of 10 on decisions)

which.job: A second reader of a timeline row's label
which.check: never the labeller: a row is flagged for the lead only when both disagree with the label

which.job: The same, when the row is hard and a few seconds do not matter
which.check: as above. Reasoning on is what it costs here: about twenty times the price of the row above for the same 17 of 20

fourth_label.title: A question for Dinis: do our three labels lack a fourth, "our measurement"?
fourth_label.by: asked by incident.conductor@web-summit.dinis (its message of 02:38 UTC), from this page's results; written up by incident.models@
fourth_label.text: The lead keeps the three labels below as they are: by our rule, anything that is our own analysis is a hypothesis. The models were given that rule and still read these rows differently, and the way they differ is the finding. Two of the rows are counts incident.media@ made from sources we hold (who published when; that no article title had reported a change by a given time). The third is an absence we observed (no further statement found in a sweep). None is an opinion or a forecast-like reading: each can be recomputed from the dataset it names and would come out the same. Our labels have fact (read at the body that decides, warns or measures), evidence (reported by others) and hypothesis (our reasoning, with its reasons). A count we made ourselves sits in none of them comfortably: it is not the primary source's statement, not someone else's report, and not a judgement. A fourth kind, "our measurement" (we counted or computed it from sources we hold; reproducible; with its limits stated), would let a reader tell the meteorologist's 'the centre most likely passes just south of Lisbon' from the media desk's '87 of 212 items carry Lusa's by-line'. Today both wear the same word. No row has been relabelled.

per_100: So a second reader on every row of a 100-row timeline costs under one US cent on the two large open-weight models that answer without reasoning (Gemma 4 31B, Llama 4 Maverick), and 30 to 60 cents on the two that reason at length by default. Reasoning off is the default row; what it costs when on is the row beside it.

per_model.google/gemma-3-4b-it: Translation at volume and nothing else. It kept every figure in all 20 warning texts for 0.0005 US dollars per 100, and copied CAP fields perfectly; it got 8 of 20 labels and 3 of 10 decisions (it invents hours and deciders), and none of the harder warnings items it reached. A 4-billion-parameter model: usable where a mechanical check (the figures check) stands behind every output.
per_model.openai/gpt-oss-20b: A reasonable small model for extraction where a second model checks it: 9 of 10 decisions, 20 of 20 translations, 15 of 20 labels. It always reasons (the provider will not turn it off), so it is slower than its size suggests (2 to 20 seconds), and on the harder warnings task it ran out of tokens on 4 of the 8 calls it got to make. Apache 2.0, so it could be run on our own machine: the one small model here where that is both allowed without conditions and worth testing.
per_model.mistralai/ministral-8b-2512: Not for our jobs as asked. It answers fast and cheaply but did not follow the output format on translation (nested JSON instead of a sentence: 0 of 20 by our rule, though the figures were there), invented hours on two decisions, and got none of the 13 harder warnings items in any of three runs.
per_model.qwen/qwen3.5-9b: With reasoning off: translation only (20 of 20). With reasoning on it is better where a rule is weighed (decisions 9 of 10 against 6) but takes 20 to 30 seconds an item and runs out of tokens on longer texts. For the same money and time a larger model that does not reason does better.
per_model.google/gemma-4-31b-it: Our default open-weight model for this site's jobs. 10 of 10 decisions, 20 of 20 translations, 17 of 20 labels, and the only row to finish the harder warnings task well without reasoning (11 of 13, the same in three runs), at about a third of a cent per 100 items and under 2 seconds. Apache 2.0. Every output still passes its check (a second model, the figures check) before use.
per_model.meta-llama/llama-4-maverick: Equal to Gemma 4 on the round-1 tasks (10 of 10, 20 of 20, 17 of 20) and fast, so a good second reader beside it. But on the harder warnings task (compare times across seventeen messages) it got 1 or 2 of 13: not for anything that needs several records weighed at once. Meta's own licence, not a standard open-source one.
per_model.deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash: The open-weight model to call when a row or a text is hard and a few seconds do not matter: with reasoning on (its default) it got 10 of 10 decisions, 20 of 20 translations, 17 of 20 labels and all 11 of the harder warnings items it reached. That costs about twenty times Gemma 4 per label. With reasoning off it was asked only part of one task before the credits ran out. MIT licence.
per_model.qwen/qwen3.5-397b-a17b: Only with reasoning off. At its default it reasons at great length: the dearest row here (half a US cent an item, 10 to 25 seconds) and it ran out of tokens on 4 of 20 translations. With reasoning off it matched the best on decisions (10 of 10) and translation (17 of 17 answered) at a fourteenth to a seventieth of the price. Nothing it does here is not done as well by Gemma 4 for less.
per_model.mistralai/mistral-large-4-0: Accurate (10 of 10 decisions, 17 of 20 labels, 19 of 20 translations) and dear for it: it reasons on every call and the provider refuses to turn that off, so it cost about a third of a US cent an item and 5 to 7 seconds. No job here needs it over Gemma 4 or DeepSeek. Its licence is Mistral's own: open weights, with conditions for anyone selling it as a service.
per_model.openai/gpt-6-luna: A cheap commercial second reader: 20 of 20 translations, 16 of 20 labels, 9 of 10 decisions (it named the Government as the decider of Web Summit's own decision), and 8 of the 9 harder warnings items it reached. About the price of the open-weight models. No reason to prefer it to them here, and no reason to avoid it as the second opinion from a different maker.
per_model.google/gemini-3.5-flash-lite: The commercial model we would pair with Gemma 4 as the second opinion on decisions: 10 of 10, 20 of 20 translations, 17 of 20 labels, under a second. It always reasons a little (the provider will not turn it off). It was not reached on the harder task before the credits ran out.
per_model.anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5: Accurate on extraction and translation (10 of 10, 20 of 20) and the most cautious on labels (15 of 20: it calls our own checks evidence). A sound second reader at about a cent per 100 rows. One harder warnings item reached, right in each of three runs: too little to say more.
per_model.openai/gpt-6.1-terra: The largest commercial model here, and on these small jobs no better than the cheap ones (10 of 10, 20 of 20, 16 of 20) at seven to ten times their price. Its place would be the tasks that are still hard for the others; the harder task did not reach it before the credits ran out.
